figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. Adenylation-thiolation-thioesterase (A-T-TE) tridomain NRPS-like enzymes and the unique function of the TE domain of D-
alanyltransferase AstC. (A) Sequence similarity network (SSN) analysis of A-T-TE-type single-module NRPSs. AstC served as a representative enzyme
catalyzing intermolecular esterification. AtrA, TdiA, AcyN, PngA, ApvA, BtyA, AtqA, and MelA were representative enzymes catalyzing the
dimerization of diverse α-keto acids in fungi, while EchA was found in Streptomyces. PacP was an A-T-TE tridomain NRPS with an inactive TE domain.
Details of these enzymes are listed in Table S4. The gray dots represent atypical enzymes with unknown functions. (B) AstC TE independently
catalyzed the intermolecular esterification between trienomycinol (1) and D-alanyl SNAC. (C) Phylogenetic analysis and functional diversity of
representative type I TEs of NRPSs. Details of the TEs are listed in Table S5. The TE domain of erythromycin polyketide synthase (DEBS TE) was
used as the outgroup. (D) Catalytic triad of AstC TE consisted of Ser-Asn-His instead of the conventional Ser-Asp-His. The sequence alignment of TEs
was performed with Clustal Omega and ESPript 3. The activities of the wild-type enzyme (WT) and its mutants were detected by HPLC analysis.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Functional exploration of the D-alanyltransferases. (A) Substrate scope of AstC TE for acyl donors. Diverse acyl SNACs were employed in the
acylation of trienomycinol (1) catalyzed by AstC TE. The relative catalytic ratios of the acylated products were determined through the integration of
the LC-ESI-MS extracted ion current (EIC) peak areas, with D-alanyl loading set as 100%, respectively (Figure S4). (B) Substrate scope of AstC for
polyketide backbones. Using D-alanine as the acyl donor, two octaketide ansamycins (N-desmethyl-4,5-desepoxymaytansinol and 9-O-methyl DDM)
and two pentaketide ansamycins (microansamycin E and aminoansamycin A) were detected as the acyl acceptors, respectively, but maytansinol was
not. The hydroxyl groups used by D-alanylation are marked in pink. (C) Phylogenetic tree of homologs of AstC. The homologs in the phylogenetic tree
correspond to enzymes clustered with AstC in the SSN analysis, displaying >75% sequence similarity (Table S6). (D) X-ray crystal structure of SyAstC
A domain complexed with 5′-O-[N-(D-alanyl) sulfamoyl] adenosine (D-Ala-SA) (PDB ID: 8WWW, Table S7).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Enzymatic characterization of SmAstC. (A) Enzymatic assays of D-alanyltransferases utilizing DDM as the D-alanyl acceptor. (B) Time-
dependent variation of 3-O-D-alanyl DDM (4) in the catalysis of SmAstC. To better illustrate the changes in the enzyme activity product during the
initial stages of the reaction, a logarithmic scale was used to represent the time axis. (C) Stability assessment of 4 under varying pH conditions.
Retention of 4 was evaluated after 10-h incubation using HPLC analysis. (D) Michaelis−Menten curves depicting the catalysis of SmAstC with D-
alanine, trienomycinol (1), and DDM (3), respectively. Data are representative of three independent experiments, and values are expressed in mean ±
SEM.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Overexpression of the smastC gene in the HGF052 strain resulted in the accumulation of maytansinol. (A) HPLC profiles and EIC analysis of
the metabolites of HGFS01. The HGF052 strain predominantly produced DDM (3), accompanied by trace amounts of maytansinol (5). The
HGFS01 strain was generated through the overexpression of the smastC gene in the HGF052 strain. (B) Speculative biosynthetic process of
maytansinol in the HGFS01 strain. The first row represented the biosynthetic pathway from DDM to ansamitocin, with the pathway colored in green
representing the putative biosynthetic process of maytansinol in vivo. Compounds 9a and 9b were the side products of the HGFS01 strain (Figures S16
and S17). (C) Production enhancement of maytansinol in the HGFS01 strain with the addition of D-alanine (*p < 0.1). YMGA represents YMG agar
media supplemented with 5 mM D-alanine.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Rational design of SmAstC TE domain for enhanced catalytic efficiency toward DDM (3). (A) SmAstC TE catalyzed the intermolecular
esterification between D-alanyl SNAC and DDM. (B) Covalent docking of SmAstC TE with 3-O-D-alanyl DDM (4) to simulate the intermediate state
of D-alanylation. The ligand was covalently attached to S90 residue. (C) Enzymatic assays of mutants designed with the Funclib server. Details of the
mutants are listed in Table S13. (D) Enzymatic assays of mutants with residues mutated on the exterior side of the binding pocket. The K125 residue at
the entrance of the acyl acceptor binding pocket significantly influenced enzyme activity. (E) Kinetic analysis of SmAstCM compared to that of
SmAstC.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 6. Optimization strategies to improve maytansinol production. (A) HPLC profiles of the metabolites of recombinant strains. All of the
recombinant strains were constructed based on HGFS04, a high-yield DDM-producing strain achieved by overexpressing the asm18 gene in HGF052,
and were detected by the metabolites with a solid-state fermentation with YMGA medium. The final optimized strain, HGFS08, was employed for
scale-up fermentation in a bioreactor using LA liquid medium. (B) Mimic DEBS enzyme assembly line strategy to assemble SmAstCM, Asm11, and
Asm10. (C) Yields of maytansinol in different recombinant strains revealed by HPLC analysis (**p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001).
